html:
In 166 BCE Rome gave the small Aegean island of Delos to Athens and declared it a free port, where ships paid no harbour dues.

The aim was to punish Rhodes, which Rome felt had leaned towards Perseus of Macedon before the Battle of Pydna. Rhodes lived on its harbour taxes, and its income fell sharply as traders moved to Delos.

Delos boomed for about eighty years. Merchants from Italy, Syria, Egypt and Phoenicia built warehouses, guild halls and temples to their own gods there. It became the great slave market of the eastern Mediterranean: the geographer Strabo claimed it could handle ten thousand slaves in a day. Many of them went to the estates of Italy and Sicily, where slave revolts like the First Servile War soon broke out.

The boom ended in violence. Forces of Mithridates VI of Pontus sacked the island in 88 BCE, killing many of its Italian traders, and pirates raided it again in 69 BCE. It never recovered.
sum: In 166 BCE Rome gave the small Aegean island of Delos to Athens and declared it a free port, where ships paid no harbour dues.
